final_proof:
**Conventions.** A line $L$ through the origin making angle $\alpha$ with the $x$-axis is the set $L=\{t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha): t\in\mathbb R\}$. Replacing $\alpha$ by $\alpha+\pi$ gives the same line (replace $t$ by $-t$), and $\tan$ has period $\pi$, so everything below depends only on $\alpha \bmod \pi$; the condition "$\alpha=\pi/2$" is read modulo $\pi$, i.e. it means $\cos\alpha=0$. For $P=(x,y)$, the line through $P$ parallel to $N$ is $N_P=\{(x,y)+s(\cos\phi,\sin\phi): s\in\mathbb R\}$.

**Lemma 1 (description of the lines).**
(a) If $\cos\alpha=0$, then $L=\{(0,Y):Y\in\mathbb R\}$ (the $y$-axis), since $t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)=(0,\pm t)$.
(b) If $\cos\alpha\ne 0$, then $L=\{(X,X\tan\alpha):X\in\mathbb R\}$: the point $t(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ equals $(X, X\tan\alpha)$ with $X=t\cos\alpha$, and conversely $(X,X\tan\alpha)$ is obtained with $t=X/\cos\alpha$.
(c) Likewise $N_P=\{(x,Y):Y\in\mathbb R\}$ if $\cos\phi=0$, and $N_P=\{(X,\,y+(X-x)\tan\phi):X\in\mathbb R\}$ if $\cos\phi\ne0$ (put $X=x+s\cos\phi$, so $s\sin\phi=(X-x)\tan\phi$).

**Lemma 2 (distinctness).** Since $M\ne N$, $\theta\not\equiv\phi \pmod\pi$. Hence $\cos\theta$ and $\cos\phi$ are not both $0$ (that would force $\theta\equiv\phi\equiv\pi/2$), and if $\cos\theta\ne0\ne\cos\phi$ then $\tan\theta\ne\tan\phi$: indeed $\tan\theta=\tan\phi$ gives $\sin\theta\cos\phi-\cos\theta\sin\phi=\sin(\theta-\phi)=0$, i.e. $\theta\equiv\phi\pmod\pi$, contradiction.

So exactly one of the following three cases occurs, matching the three cases of the statement. In each case we show $M\cap N_P$ consists of exactly one point and compute it; this also shows $\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}$ is well defined.

**Case 1: $\theta=\pi/2$.** Then $\cos\phi\ne0$ by Lemma 2. By Lemma 1, $M$ is the $y$-axis and $N_P=\{(X,y+(X-x)\tan\phi)\}$. A point of $N_P$ lies on $M$ iff its first coordinate is $X=0$, which gives the unique point $(0,\,y-x\tan\phi)$. Hence $\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(0,\,y-x\tan\phi)$.

**Case 2: $\phi=\pi/2$.** Then $\cos\theta\ne0$. By Lemma 1, $N_P=\{(x,Y)\}$ and $M=\{(X,X\tan\theta)\}$. A point $(X,X\tan\theta)$ of $M$ lies on $N_P$ iff $X=x$, giving the unique point $(x,\,x\tan\theta)$. Hence $\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=(x,\,x\tan\theta)$.

**Case 3: otherwise** ($\cos\theta\ne0$, $\cos\phi\ne0$, so $\tan\theta\ne\tan\phi$). A point lies in $M\cap N_P$ iff it has the form $(X,Y)$ with $Y=X\tan\theta$ and $Y=y+(X-x)\tan\phi$ (the $X$-coordinate parametrizes both lines bijectively). Eliminating $Y$:
$$X\tan\theta=y+X\tan\phi-x\tan\phi\iff X(\tan\phi-\tan\theta)=x\tan\phi-y .$$
Since $\tan\phi-\tan\theta\ne0$, there is exactly one solution
$$X=\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}-\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta},$$
and then
$$Y=X\tan\theta=\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi-y\tan\theta}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}=\frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}-\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi},$$
(multiplying numerator and denominator by $-1$). Conversely this $(X,Y)$ satisfies both equations, so it is the unique intersection point. Thus
$$\operatorname{pr}_{M,N}(P)=\left(\frac{x\tan\phi}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta}-\frac{y}{\tan\phi-\tan\theta},\ \frac{y\tan\theta}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}-\frac{x\tan\theta\tan\phi}{\tan\theta-\tan\phi}\right).$$

The three cases together give exactly the claimed formula. $\blacksquare$
